questions.question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Heraka Movement - West Bengal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Heraka Movement **was not based in West Bengal but originated in the **Naga Hills of Assam and Nagaland**.
 
• This socio-religious movement was led by **Jadonang and later Rani Gaidinliu** with the aim of reviving Naga traditions and customs.
 
• The movement also sought to oppose British colonial rule and Christian missionary influence in the region.
 
• Heraka, meaning "pure," was a reformist movement that sought to consolidate the indigenous Naga religious practices and reject foreign influence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ramosi Rebellion**

 
 
• The Ramosi Rebellion (1822-1841) took place in **Maharashtra**.
 
• It led by Chittur Singh and Umaji Naik, was a response to British annexation policies in the Western Ghats.
 
• The Ramosis were a tribal community employed as hill police during Maratha rule but were marginalized under British rule.
 
 
 
• **Lushai Revolt**
 
 
• This revolt occurred in the **present-day Mizoram (then part of Assam)** during the 19th century.
 
• The Lushai tribes resisted British interference in their territory and culture.
 
• The British eventually subdued the rebellion and brought the region under their control.
 
 
 
• **Kol Rebellion**
 
 
• The Kol Rebellion (1831-1832) was centered in **Jharkhand**.
 
• The rebellion was led by the Kol tribal community against exploitative landlords and moneylenders.
 
• It was a significant tribal uprising during British colonial rule.
 
 
 
• **Heraka Movement Leadership**
 
 
• **Jadonang** was the founder of the Heraka Movement and sought to preserve Naga culture.
 
• After his execution by the British, **Rani Gaidinliu** became the leader and continued the fight for Naga identity and freedom.
 
• Rani Gaidinliu is remembered as a freedom fighter and was posthumously awarded the **Padma Bhushan**.

questions.question: Which Act transferred the power of governance from the East India Company to the British Crown?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Government of India Act, 1858**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Government of India Act, 1858** marked the end of the East India Company’s rule and transferred the administration of India directly to the British Crown.
 
• The act established the position of a **Secretary of State for India**, who was responsible for overseeing Indian affairs in Britain.
 
• It introduced the **Council of India** to assist the Secretary of State, comprising 15 members, mainly former directors of the East India Company.
 
• This act formally ended the dual governance system and centralized power under the British government, following the failure of the East India Company during the **1857 Revolt**.
 
• The Governor-General of India was renamed as **Viceroy of India**, representing the Crown directly in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Charter Act, 1833**

 
 
• This act centralized legislative powers in India by establishing a single legislative council for all British territories in India.
 
• It marked the end of the East India Company's trading rights and made it an administrative body.
 
• It introduced the idea of an open competition for civil services, but the provision was not implemented until later.
 
 
 
• **Regulating Act, 1773**
 
 
• This was the first attempt by the British government to regulate the affairs of the East India Company in India.
 
• It established a Governor-General in Bengal and created a Supreme Court at Fort William, Kolkata.
 
• The act aimed to curb corruption and mismanagement but had limited success.
 
 
 
• **Pitt's India Act, 1784**
 
 
• This act introduced the concept of dual control between the British government and the East India Company.
 
• It created a Board of Control to supervise civil, military, and revenue administration in India.
 
• The act aimed to address issues of governance after the shortcomings of the Regulating Act.
 
 
 
• **Indian Rebellion of 1857**
 
 
• The widespread uprising against British rule revealed the flaws in the East India Company's administrative structure.
 
• It directly led to the implementation of the Government of India Act, 1858, which centralized power under the Crown.
 
• The rebellion is considered one of the most significant events in Indian history, leading to the dissolution of the East India Company.

questions.question: Which act stated that the Presidencies of Madras and Bombay were to be subordinate to the Presidency of Bengal in all matters of war, diplomatic relations and revenue?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pitts' India Act, 1784**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Pitts' India Act, 1784 was enacted to bring more control and accountability in the administration of British territories in India.
 
• It established a system where the Presidencies of Madras and Bombay were made subordinate to the Presidency of Bengal in all matters concerning war, diplomacy, and revenue.
 
• The act created a dual system of governance where the British Crown and the East India Company shared authority over Indian administration.
 
• A Board of Control was set up to oversee political affairs, while the Court of Directors retained control over commercial activities.
 
• It marked a significant step towards centralized governance in British India under the Presidency of Bengal.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Presidency System:** British India was divided into three presidencies—Bengal, Madras, and Bombay—each governed by its own administration.
 
• **Board of Control:** Established by Pitts' India Act, it consisted of six members, including the British Cabinet Ministers, to oversee political governance in India.
 
• **Dual System of Governance:** Authority over India was shared between the Crown (through the Board of Control) and the East India Company (through the Court of Directors).
 
• **Revenue Administration:** Subordination of Madras and Bombay to Bengal helped establish a centralized mechanism for managing revenue collection and financial affairs.
 
• **Impact of the Act:** It strengthened British control over India and laid the foundation for future legislative acts aimed at consolidating imperial governance.

questions.question: Commercial crops were prioritised over food crops during colonial rule. Which of the following is an example of a commercial crop promoted by the British?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Indigo**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Indigo was one of the most significant commercial crops promoted by the British during colonial rule.
 
• The British encouraged indigo cultivation extensively as it was highly profitable and in demand for dyeing textiles in Europe.
 
• Farmers were often forced into growing indigo under exploitative conditions through the "Tinkathia System," where they had to dedicate a portion of their land to indigo crops.
 
• Indigo cultivation led to the exploitation of Indian farmers, causing widespread resentment and eventually leading to the Indigo Revolt (1859-1860).
 
• The prioritization of indigo and other commercial crops severely impacted food crop production, leading to famines and food shortages during colonial rule.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Commercial Crops:** These are crops grown primarily for sale and profit rather than for subsistence. Examples include indigo, cotton, jute, and tea.
 
• **Indigo Revolt:** A major uprising by farmers in Bengal in 1859-1860 against forced cultivation of indigo and exploitative practices by British planters.
 
• **Tinkathia System:** A system imposed by British planters where farmers had to grow indigo on 3/20th of their land compulsorily, often leading to financial distress.
 
• **Impact on Food Crops:** The emphasis on commercial crop cultivation displaced food crops, contributing to famines such as the Great Bengal Famine of 1943.
 
• **Colonial Agricultural Policies:** The British prioritized cash crops for export, neglecting the needs of local populations, which caused significant socio-economic hardships in rural India.

questions.question: The Paramhansa Sabha was founded in:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1849**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Paramhansa Sabha was founded in **1849** in Maharashtra as a secret socio-religious reform society.
 
• It was started by **Dadoba Pandurang**, along with his associates, with the aim of promoting social and religious reforms.
 
• The Sabha focused on **abolishing caste discrimination** and promoting equality within society.
 
• It emphasized the study of religious texts, spreading knowledge, and creating a sense of brotherhood among people.
 
• The Sabha played a crucial role in laying the foundation for later reform movements, such as the **Prarthana Samaj**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dadoba Pandurang Tarkhadkar:** A key figure in the socio-religious reform movement in Maharashtra, known for his efforts in promoting liberal thought and education.
 
• **Prarthana Samaj:** Inspired by the Paramhansa Sabha, this organization was later founded in 1867 with a focus on social reform and religious rationalism.
 
• **Social Reform Movements in India:** The 19th century saw a wave of reform movements aimed at eradicating social evils like caste discrimination, child marriage, and sati.
 
• **Secret Societies for Reform:** Many early reform initiatives, like the Paramhansa Sabha, operated in secrecy to avoid opposition from orthodox sections of society.
 
• **Legacy of Paramhansa Sabha:** It influenced other reform movements and became a precursor to organizations advocating for equality, education, and rationalism in India.

questions.question: Which of the given tribal uprisings did NOT take place around the unrest during the Revolt of 1857?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Birsa Munda Revolt**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Birsa Munda Revolt**, also known as the Ulgulan (The Great Tumult), occurred in the late 19th century (1899–1900) and was not connected to the Revolt of 1857.
 
• This revolt was led by **Birsa Munda**, a tribal leader from the Munda community, in the Chotanagpur region (present-day Jharkhand).
 
• The rebellion primarily aimed at resisting British colonial exploitation and missionary interference in tribal lands and culture.
 
• Birsa Munda's movement focused on the restoration of tribal rights over their land (Khuntkatti system) and rejecting oppressive British laws.
 
• Unlike the other uprisings mentioned, which were closely linked to the broader unrest during the Revolt of 1857, the Birsa Munda Revolt was a localized tribal movement in the late 19th century.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rebellion of Sambalpur (1857–1864):**

 
 
• This revolt was led by Veer Surendra Sai against British rule in Sambalpur (present-day Odisha).
 
• It was closely linked to the larger Revolt of 1857 and aimed at overthrowing British authority in the region.
 
• Surendra Sai fought for the restoration of local tribal and princely rights.
 
 
 
• **Naikda Movement (1857–1858):**
 
 
• This tribal uprising occurred in Gujarat during the Revolt of 1857.
 
• The Naikda tribe resisted British policies that disrupted their traditional lifestyle and autonomy.
 
• It was a localized movement but inspired by the general anti-colonial sentiment of 1857.
 
 
 
• **Santhal Rebellion (1855–1856):**
 
 
• Led by Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu, the Santhal Rebellion took place in the Rajmahal Hills (present-day Jharkhand).
 
• It was a precursor to the Revolt of 1857 and aimed at resisting oppressive zamindari systems and British policies.
 
• The Santhal tribes fought for their rights to land and freedom from exploitative moneylenders.
 
 
 
• **Tribal Movements in India:**
 
 
• Tribal uprisings were often reactions to exploitation by British policies, zamindars, and moneylenders.
 
• Most tribal revolts were rooted in issues like land alienation, forced labor, and cultural interference.
 
• These movements highlight the resilience and struggles of indigenous communities against colonial oppression.

questions.question: In which year did the English East India Company pass a new law that required every new person who took up employment in the Company’s army to serve overseas if required?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1856**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In **1856**, the English East India Company passed a law mandating that soldiers employed in its army had to serve overseas if required.
 
• This law was significant as it challenged the traditional beliefs of Indian sepoys, particularly regarding crossing the seas, which was considered against their religious practices.
 
• The resentment caused by this law among Indian soldiers contributed to the growing unrest that eventually culminated in the **Revolt of 1857**.
 
• This regulation was part of the larger socio-political changes introduced by the British to consolidate their control over India.
 
• The law showcased the disregard of the British towards local cultural sensitivities, leading to widespread dissatisfaction among Indian troops.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Revolt of 1857:**

 
 
• The revolt was triggered by multiple factors, including resentment over policies like the overseas service law and the introduction of Enfield rifles with cartridges rumored to be greased with cow and pig fat.
 
• It is considered the first major uprising against British rule in India.
 
• Both sepoys and civilians participated in the revolt, which started in Meerut and spread across northern and central India.
 
 
 
• **Cultural Sensitivities:**
 
 
• Crossing the seas was considered a religious taboo among certain Indian communities, as it was believed to result in the loss of caste.
 
• The imposition of the overseas service regulation was seen as an affront to traditional values.
 
 
 
• **English East India Company:**
 
 
• The company governed India until 1858, after which control was transferred to the British Crown.
 
• Its policies often ignored local customs, leading to widespread dissatisfaction and resistance among Indians.
 
 
 
• **Military Reforms:**
 
 
• British reforms in the Indian army aimed at aligning the forces with Western military practices.
 
• These reforms were often resisted by Indian soldiers due to cultural and religious differences.

questions.question: Which of the following acts reduced the number of directors of East India Company?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Charter Act of 1853**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Charter Act of 1853** was the last of the Charter Acts passed by the British Parliament for the East India Company.
 
• This Act reduced the number of directors of the East India Company from **24 to 18**, with six directors to be nominated by the British Crown.
 
• It marked the beginning of the separation of legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council by introducing a separate Legislative Council.
 
• The Act did not specify a fixed period for the continuation of the East India Company, unlike previous Charter Acts.
 
• It was a significant step towards the development of a parliamentary system in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Charter Act of 1833:** This Act centralized the administration in India by making the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India and abolished the monopoly of the East India Company in trade.
 
• **Charter Act of 1813:** Ended the commercial monopoly of the East India Company except for trade in tea and trade with China and allowed Christian missionaries to propagate their religion in India.
 
• **Charter Act of 1793:** Renewed the company's charter for another 20 years and allowed it to retain its monopoly on trade in India.
 
• **Governor-General's Council:** The Charter Act of 1853 expanded the Governor-General's Council to include six new legislative members, paving the way for greater legislative deliberation.
 
• **Impact:** The Act is considered a precursor to the Indian Councils Act of 1861, which further reformed the legislative structure in British India.

questions.question: Who founded the Prarthana Samaj?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Atmaram Pandurang**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Atmaram Pandurang** was the founder of the **Prarthana Samaj**, established in **1867** in Bombay (now Mumbai).
 
• The Prarthana Samaj was influenced by the ideas of the **Brahmo Samaj** and focused on **social and religious reform**.
 
• It emphasized **monotheism** and opposed idol worship and caste discrimination.
 
• Atmaram Pandurang was supported by prominent leaders like **Justice Mahadev Govind Ranade** in propagating the ideals of the Prarthana Samaj.
 
• The movement aimed at creating a society based on rational thought, equality, and ethical principles, paving the way for modern reformist ideologies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Brahmo Samaj:** Founded by **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** in 1828, it laid the foundation for religious and social reform movements in India.
 
• **Justice Mahadev Govind Ranade:** A key figure in the Prarthana Samaj, Ranade worked towards abolishing caste discrimination and promoting women’s education and widow remarriage.
 
• **Social Reform Movements:** The Prarthana Samaj was part of a broader reformist wave in 19th century India aimed at eradicating social evils like untouchability, child marriage, and gender inequality.
 
• **Religious Philosophy:** The Samaj advocated a rational approach to religion, promoting ethical living and humanitarian values over ritualistic practices.
 
• **Legacy:** The efforts of the Prarthana Samaj contributed significantly to the modernization of Indian society and the spread of progressive ideas during the colonial era.

questions.question: Which of the following tribal uprising leaders was/were NOT executed during the revolt but deported to another country?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Tirot Sing**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Tirot Sing**, also known as **Tirot Sing Syiem**, was a tribal chief of the **Khasi people** in the northeastern region of India (modern-day Meghalaya).
 
• He led the resistance against the **British colonial forces** in the 19th century when they attempted to control Khasi hills through treaties and military power.
 
• Tirot Sing was not executed after his capture. Instead, he was **deported to Dhaka (present-day Bangladesh)**, where he eventually died in captivity in 1835.
 
• He is considered a **symbol of bravery and resistance** against British colonialism in the northeastern part of India.
 
• The **state of Meghalaya** honors his memory with a **state holiday on 17th July**, celebrated as **Tirot Sing Day**.
 
• Tirot Sing's legacy is a reminder of the **indigenous resistance** to colonial exploitation and the preservation of regional autonomy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Nilamber and Pitamber**__

 __
 
• **Nilamber and Pitamber** were brothers who led the **Kol uprising** against British forces in the region of present-day Jharkhand.
 
• Both brothers were **captured and executed** by the British in **1859**.
 
• The Kol uprising was one of the most significant tribal revolts in the history of India.
 
 
 
• **Tilka Manjhi**__
 __
 
• **Tilka Manjhi** was a Santhal leader who fought against the British forces in the 18th century.
 
• He was **captured, tied to a horse, and executed** by the British in **1785**.
 
• He is often regarded as the **first tribal leader** to rise against British rule in India.
 
 
 
• **Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu**__
 
 
• **Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu** were leaders of the **Santhal rebellion** (also known as the Hul rebellion) against British rule in 1855.
 
• They were **executed** by the British after the rebellion was suppressed.
 
• The Santhal rebellion is remembered for its intensity and is a significant part of India's tribal history.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT correct with respect to the Naikdas Uprising Sankheda,1858?

options.text: They resorted to guerrilla tactics, harassing the British troops and attacking the British thanas
The revolt took place around Chhotaudepur district in Gujarat.
The leader Rupa surrendered before the British in 1860.
The Naikdas of Sankheda took arms under both the leaders Rupa Naik and K Naik

questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**The leader Rupa surrendered before the British in 1860.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Naikdas Uprising** was a significant tribal revolt that occurred in the **Sankheda region of Gujarat** in 1858.
 
• It was led by **Rupa Naik** and **K Naik**, two prominent leaders of the Naikda tribal community.
 
• The revolt was part of the larger resistance against the British during the **First War of Independence (1857).**
 
• The Naikdas used **guerrilla tactics** to harass British troops, targeting British outposts and thanas (police stations).
 
• The Naikdas primarily revolted due to their opposition to the British administration’s interference in their **traditional tribal lifestyle** and exploitation by local authorities.
 
• There is no historical evidence to suggest that **Rupa Naik surrendered** to the British in 1860, making this statement incorrect.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Guerrilla tactics**__

 __
 
• These tactics involve using **small, mobile, and flexible combat groups** to carry out surprise attacks and ambushes.
 
• The Naikdas adopted this method to counter the **better-equipped British forces**.
 
 
 
• **Chhotaudepur district**__
 __
 
• This district is located in **eastern Gujarat** and is known for its **tribal population.**
 
• The district was a key region for tribal uprisings like the Naikdas Uprising.
 
 
 
• **Naikda tribal community**__
 
 
• The Naikdas are an **indigenous tribal group** in Gujarat, known for their strong attachment to their **traditional lifestyle and customs.**
 
• Their uprisings were driven by their resistance to British-imposed reforms and exploitation.

questions.question: According to the Charter Act of 1793, the charter of the east India company was renewed for how many years?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**20 years**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Charter Act of 1793** was an important legislative act passed by the British Parliament, which renewed the **charter of the East India Company** for an additional period of **20 years**.
 
• This act maintained the **monopoly of the East India Company** in trade, particularly in the region of India, which was a significant source of revenue for the British Empire.
 
• The act also made provisions to allocate a part of the company's revenue for **civil and military expenses** incurred by the British Government in India.
 
• One of the major outcomes of the act was the emphasis on the **governance and administration** of Indian territories controlled by the East India Company.
 
• The act continued the system of **dual administration**, where the Company had administrative control but was overseen by the British Crown.
 
• It was during this period that the East India Company's role transitioned more from a commercial enterprise to an **administrative authority** in India.
 
• The act also legalized the payment of the Company's employees from Indian revenue, ensuring better management and accountability.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Key Features of the Charter Acts**__

 __
 
• The **Charter Acts** were a series of legislative acts passed by the British Parliament to regulate the governance and trade of the East India Company.
 
• The **Charter Act of 1813**, for instance, abolished the company's monopoly over trade in India, except for trade in tea and trade with China.
 
• The **Charter Act of 1833** centralized the administration of India and marked the beginning of the legislative council's work.
 
• The **Charter Act of 1853** was the last in the series and paved the way for the appointment of Indians to civil services through a competitive examination.
 
 
 
• **Importance of the East India Company**__
 
 
• The East India Company played a crucial role in the **economic and political transformation of India**.
 
• Its control over Indian territories laid the foundation for the establishment of the **British Raj** in 1858.
 
• It was instrumental in introducing various **modern reforms**, including railways, postal services, and legal systems, though often with the intention of benefiting colonial rule.

questions.question: Which colonial power held Yanaon (Yanam) and Chandernagore as part of its possessions in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**French**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Yanaon (Yanam)** and **Chandernagore** were part of the colonial possessions of France in India.
 
• The French established their presence in India in the 17th century and controlled territories like **Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahé, Yanam, and Chandernagore**.
 
• Chandernagore, located in present-day West Bengal, was an important trading post for the French East India Company.
 
• Yanam, situated in present-day Andhra Pradesh, was part of French India until its merger with the Indian Union in 1954.
 
• These territories were governed under the administrative unit of **French India** until their integration into India post-independence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **French Colonial Presence in India:**

 
 
• The French East India Company was established in 1664 to compete with British and Dutch colonial powers in trade.
 
• The French aimed to establish trading posts along the coastlines of India, starting with Surat in Gujarat.
 
• Pondicherry (now Puducherry) became the headquarters of French India in 1674.
 
 
 
• **Integration of French Territories into India:**
 
 
• After India's independence in 1947, negotiations were held between the French and Indian governments for the integration of French territories.
 
• Chandernagore joined India in 1950 through a public referendum, while Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahé, and Yanam merged in 1954.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of French India:**
 
 
• The French influence is still evident in Puducherry's architecture, culture, and cuisine.
 
• Puducherry is governed as a union territory, preserving its unique historical identity.
 
 
 
• **Other Colonial Powers in India:**
 
 
• The Portuguese controlled Goa, Daman, Diu, and Dadra & Nagar Haveli.
 
• The British ruled most of the Indian subcontinent through the British East India Company and later under direct Crown rule.
 
• The Dutch and Danish also had minor trading posts but were overshadowed by other powers.

questions.question: Which uprising in Uttar Pradesh, led by Mufti Muhammad Aiwaz, was among the most significant revolts against British rule in India prior to the First War of Independence in 1857?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bareilly Uprisings**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Bareilly Uprisings were an important revolt against British rule in India, occurring in the early 19th century, prior to the First War of Independence in 1857.
 
• These uprisings were led by Mufti Muhammad Aiwaz, who played a critical role in mobilizing resistance against British colonial policies.
 
• The revolt primarily took place in the Bareilly region of present-day Uttar Pradesh and reflected the growing unrest among Indian communities under British rule.
 
• The uprising was driven by widespread dissatisfaction with British economic exploitation, religious interference, and administrative policies.
 
• The Bareilly Uprisings are considered significant precursors to the larger and more organized rebellions that culminated in the Revolt of 1857.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Revolt of 1857:**

• The revolt was led by various leaders across regions, including Rani Lakshmibai, Tantia Tope, Bahadur Shah Zafar, and Nana Saheb.

• **Chuar Rebellion:** A series of uprisings in Bengal and Bihar during the late 18th century by tribal communities resisting British revenue collection.
 
 
 
• **Mufti Muhammad Aiwaz:**
 
 
• Mufti Muhammad Aiwaz was a prominent leader of the Bareilly Uprisings and played a crucial role in uniting people against British authority.
 
• He symbolized resistance to British interference in the religious and social practices of Indian communities.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Early Uprisings:**
 
 
• These early uprisings highlighted the growing resentment among Indians toward British policies and exploitation.
 
• They laid the foundation for organized resistance movements in the 19th and 20th centuries, culminating in India's independence in 1947.

• Eustachius De Lannoy later became a trusted military advisor to Marthanda Varma, helping modernize the Travancore army with European military techniques.
 
• This battle is a symbol of resistance against colonial domination and showcases the military prowess of Indian rulers during the pre-colonial period.

questions.question: What is Lord Thomas Babington Macaulay best known for in the context of British India?

options.text: Drafting the Indian Penal Code and promoting English education
Framing the Government of India Act, 1858

questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Drafting the Indian Penal Code and promoting English education**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Lord Thomas Babington Macaulay** was a British historian, politician, and lawmaker who played a pivotal role in shaping the administrative and educational policies of **British India**.
 
• He is best known for drafting the **Indian Penal Code (IPC)**, which became the backbone of the Indian legal system and is still in use today with modifications.
 
• The IPC was a comprehensive code of criminal law for India, and it was officially enacted in **1860**.
 
• In addition to his work on the IPC, Macaulay strongly advocated for the promotion of **English education in India**.
 
• His famous **"Minute on Education"** (1835) laid the foundation for the use of English as the medium of instruction in Indian schools and colleges.
 
• Macaulay believed that English education would create a class of Indians who were **"Indian in blood and color, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect."**
 
• His efforts significantly influenced the spread of Western education, science, and literature in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Framing the Government of India Act, 1858**__

 __
 
• The **Government of India Act, 1858** marked the formal transfer of power from the **East India Company** to the British Crown.
 
• This Act was introduced after the **Indian Rebellion of 1857** to improve governance in India.
 
• However, Macaulay was not directly involved in drafting this Act.
 
 
 
• **Introducing the Vernacular Press Act**__
 __
 
• The **Vernacular Press Act** of 1878 was introduced by **Lord Lytton**, not Macaulay.
 
• This Act aimed to curb the freedom of the Indian-language press and suppress criticism of British policies.
 
 
 
• **Leading the revolt of 1857**__
 
 
• The **Indian Rebellion of 1857** was a large-scale uprising against British rule, but Macaulay was not involved in leading it.
 
• By the time of the revolt, Macaulay had already returned to England and was not in India.

questions.question: Which institution was established in 1921 as a deliberative body for princes?

__
 
• The **Chamber of Princes** was established in the year **1921** as a **deliberative and advisory body** for the princely states in British India.
 
• It was set up by the British Government to provide a platform for the princely rulers to **discuss and deliberate matters** related to their states and their relationship with the British Crown.
 
• The Chamber of Princes was inaugurated by the then **Duke of Connaught** in 1921 at the **Rashtrapati Bhavan** (then known as the Viceroy's House).
 
• This body consisted of **108 members**, including rulers of princely states and their representatives.
 
• The Chamber was a purely advisory body and had no legislative powers, functioning as a forum for princes to **exchange ideas and communicate with the British Government.**
 
• It was a part of the British Government's attempt to **control and manage** the princely states effectively.
 
• The Chamber ceased to exist after **India’s independence in 1947** when princely states were integrated into the Indian Union.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The members of the Indian Council were based in **London** and were responsible for advising on policy matters.

• It may appear to suggest a legislative body, but such an assembly did not exist under this name during British rule in India.

• The **Royal Consultation Board** is not a historically recognized institution under British rule in India.
 
• It does not relate to the Chamber of Princes or any similar body.

questions.question: In 1510, Alfonzo de Albuquerque captured which place from the Sultan of Bijapur and made it the capital of the Portuguese eastern empire?

__
 
• In 1510, **Alfonso de Albuquerque**, a Portuguese general and military strategist, captured Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur.
 
• Goa was strategically chosen due to its **central location on the western coast of India**, making it ideal for trade and military operations.
 
• After its capture, Goa was established as the capital of the **Portuguese eastern empire**.
 
• The Portuguese ruled Goa for over 450 years until its liberation by India in **1961**.
 
• Albuquerque is regarded as one of the key figures in establishing Portuguese colonial dominance in Asia.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Portuguese Empire in India:**

 
 
• The Portuguese first arrived in India in 1498, led by Vasco da Gama.
 
• Goa became the center of Portuguese trade and administration in Asia.
 
• Other Portuguese territories in India included Daman, Diu, and Dadra Nagar Haveli.
 
 
 
• **Alfonso de Albuquerque:**
 
 
• Albuquerque served as the second Governor of Portuguese India from 1509 to 1515.
 
• He is known as the architect of the Portuguese colonial empire in Asia.
 
• He implemented policies to fortify and expand Portuguese territories in the region.
 
 
 
• **Historical Importance of Goa:**
 
 
• Goa served as a major hub for spice trade, connecting Europe with Asia.

questions.question: Which of the following acts of the East India Company formally separated the Legislative and Executive functions of Governor-General’s Council?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Charter Act of 1853**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Charter Act of 1853** was the last in the series of Charter Acts passed by the British Parliament for the governance of India.
 
• This Act formally **separated the legislative and executive functions** of the Governor-General’s Council.
 
• A separate **Legislative Council** was created under this Act, marking the beginning of a distinct legislative machinery in British India.
 
• The Governor-General’s Council now had six members—four executive and two legislative members.
 
• The Act also allowed Indians to be appointed to the Legislative Council for the first time, although their participation was limited.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Charter Act of 1833:**

 
 
• It made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India, centralizing administration.
 
• It ended the commercial operations of the East India Company and made it a purely administrative body.
 
• The Act attempted to introduce open competition for civil services but faced opposition.
 
 
 
• **Key Terminology:**
 
 
• **Governor-General's Council:** The council was an advisory body assisting the Governor-General in administrative and legislative matters.
 
• **Legislative Council:** A body created for enacting laws, distinct from the executive functions of the government.
 
 
 
• **Role of the East India Company:**
 
 
• The East India Company initially held both administrative and commercial powers in India.
 
• The Charter Acts progressively curbed its commercial role and enhanced its administrative authority under British Parliament's control.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Charter Act of 1853:**
 
 
• It marked a step towards modern legislative practices in India.
 
• The Act laid the groundwork for subsequent reforms, including the Indian Councils Act of 1861.

questions.question: According to the Regulating Act 1773, which of the following options is INCORRECT about the powers and responsibilities of the Governor General?

options.text: Can make rules and regulations for the civil government of Fort William

Powered to superintendent the presidencies of Madras and Bombay in war and peace
Can override the decision of his council

questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Regulating Act of 1773 established the office of the Governor-General of Bengal, who was assisted by an executive council of four members.
 
• The Governor-General was empowered to make rules and regulations for the civil government of Fort William in Bengal.
 
• The Governor-General had the power to control and superintend the presidencies of Madras and Bombay in matters of war and peace.
 
• However, the Governor-General could not override the decision of his council; decisions were to be taken collectively, and in the event of a tie, the Governor-General held the casting vote.
 
• This limitation was an attempt to ensure checks and balances within the colonial administration.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Regulating Act of 1773:**

 
 
• The first attempt by the British Parliament to regulate the affairs of the East India Company and its territories in India.
 
• It marked the beginning of parliamentary control over the Company's administration in India.
 
• It restricted the private trade of Company officials and sought to address administrative corruption.
 
 
 
• **Governor-General of Bengal:**
 
 
• The Regulating Act designated the Governor of Bengal as the Governor-General of Bengal.
 
• Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General under the Act.
 
 
 
• **Executive Council:**
 
 
• The Governor-General's Executive Council consisted of four members appointed by the Court of Directors of the East India Company.
 
• It functioned as a decision-making body, with the Governor-General having the casting vote.
 
 
 
• **Limitations of the Regulating Act:**
 
 
• The Act failed to provide adequate checks on the Governor-General's powers.
 
• Conflicts often arose between the Governor-General and his council members due to the lack of clarity in decision-making authority.
 
• This led to the enactment of the Pitt's India Act of 1784, which introduced further reforms.

• The **Dikus** often manipulated tribal people into debt through unfair lending practices and forced them to work in bonded labor.
 
• The tribal communities, who primarily depended on the forest for their livelihood, faced hardships as the **Dikus extracted resources** and restricted access to forests.
 
• The interference of the **Dikus** led to the erosion of tribal autonomy and culture, creating resentment among the tribes.
 
• This oppression and exploitation by the **Dikus** became a major factor in igniting several **early tribal revolts** in India, such as the **Santhal Rebellion (1855-56)** and the **Munda Rebellion (1899-1900)**.

questions.question: Which body was established to control all matters of civil and military government of British territories in India?

__
 
• The **Board of Control** was established under the **Pitt's India Act of 1784**.
 
• This act was introduced to ensure better governance of the **British territories in India**.
 
• The board had the authority to oversee and direct all matters related to the **civil and military government** in British India.
 
• It functioned alongside the **Court of Directors of the East India Company**, ensuring a balance between the British Crown and the Company.
 
• The Board of Control consisted of **six members**, including the **Chancellor of the Exchequer** and the **Secretary of State**.
 
• It was responsible for formulating policies related to **administration, trade, and military** in India.
 
• This mechanism marked a significant shift, as it gave the British Crown greater control over the **Company's affairs** in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 __

• It might signify a legislative assembly or governing body responsible for enacting laws, but it is not related to the governance structure established under the **Pitt's India Act.**
 
 
 
• **Board of Executives**__
 __
 
• No official body named **Board of Executives** existed in the context of British India.
 
• The term could refer to an executive committee or governing body in general, but it is not relevant to the governance mechanism established by the British Crown for India.
 
 
 
• **Board of Directors**__
 
 
• The **Board of Directors** was part of the East India Company and responsible for managing the company's business affairs.
 
• While it played a key role in trade and commercial decisions, it did not oversee matters of **civil and military governance.**

questions.question: In which year was English education formally introduced in India by the British?

__
 
• The formal introduction of **English education** in India by the British took place in the year **1835**.
 
• This decision was largely influenced by the ideas of **Thomas Babington Macaulay**, who advocated for the promotion of English education in his famous **Minute on Education**.
 
• Macaulay argued that English education would create a class of Indians who were **"Indian in blood and color, but English in taste, opinions, morals, and intellect."**
 
• The **Charter Act of 1813** had earlier allowed for the allocation of funds to promote education in India, but it was in **1835** that the focus shifted explicitly to English education.
 
• As a result of this shift, the British introduced English as the medium of instruction in schools and colleges, particularly in higher education.
 
• Institutions such as the **Calcutta Medical College** (established in 1835) began using English as the primary medium of teaching.
 
• This marked the beginning of a significant cultural and educational transformation in India, with English becoming a key language for administration, education, and intellectual discourse.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **1813**__

 __
 
• The **Charter Act of 1813** marked the first step by the British to involve themselves in the promotion of education in India.
 
• It allocated a sum of **1 lakh rupees annually** for the "revival and promotion of literature" and the introduction of "useful knowledge" in India.
 
• However, no specific emphasis on English education was made under this act.
 
 
 
• **1854**__
 __
 
• The year **1854** is significant for the **Wood's Despatch**, which laid the foundation for the modern education system in India.
 
• It recommended the establishment of **universities in Bombay, Calcutta, and Madras** and proposed a system of education at all levels (primary, secondary, and higher).
 
• The despatch also emphasized the use of both English and vernacular languages in education.
 
 
 
• **1829**__
 
 
• The year **1829** is historically significant for the abolition of **Sati** under the efforts of **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** and Governor-General **Lord William Bentinck**.
 
• It does not directly relate to the introduction of English education in India.

__

• This change marked the formal transfer of authority from the **East India Company to the British Crown**, after the events of the Revolt of 1857 (also called the First War of Independence).
 
• The Viceroy acted as the **direct representative of the British Crown** and was responsible for administering India on behalf of the monarch.

• The **Government of India Act 1858** was a significant legislative change that centralized governance under the Crown, ending the dual control system of the East India Company.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Revolt of 1857:**

 
 
• Also known as India's First War of Independence, it was a major uprising against the rule of the British East India Company.
 
• The revolt led to significant political changes, including the abolition of the East India Company's rule in India.
 
 
 
• **Government of India Act 1858:**
 
 
• This act abolished the East India Company's authority and transferred governance directly to the British Crown.
 
• A new office called the "Secretary of State for India" was created to oversee Indian administration from Britain.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Viceroy:**
 
 
• The Viceroy served as the head of the colonial administration in India.
 
• He was responsible for implementing policies and laws on behalf of the British Crown.
 
 
 
• **Lord Canning:**
 
 
• He was the last Governor-General of India under the East India Company.
 
• He became the first Viceroy of India after the Government of India Act 1858 came into effect.
 
 
 
• **Significance of 1858:**
 
 
• The transition symbolized the beginning of the British Crown’s direct rule over India, which lasted until Indian independence in 1947.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of reform organisations and their founders is correctly matched?

options.text: Arya Samaj - Raja Ram Mohan Roy

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Satya Shodhak Samaj - Jyotiba Phule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Satya Shodhak Samaj** was founded by Jyotiba Phule in 1873 in Pune, Maharashtra, with the aim of promoting social equality and challenging caste-based discrimination.
 
• The organization focused on uplifting marginalized sections of society, including lower castes and women, by spreading education and awareness about their rights.
 
• It opposed the dominance of the Brahminical priesthood and sought to challenge the rigid caste hierarchy prevalent in Indian society at the time.
 
• Jyotiba Phule and his wife, Savitribai Phule, actively worked to provide education to women and oppressed communities, believing that education was the key to social reform.
 
• Satya Shodhak Samaj also emphasized self-respect, rational thinking, and the rejection of blind faith and superstitions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Brahmo Samaj:**

 
 
• Founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy in 1828, it aimed at reforming Hindu society by abolishing practices like Sati and promoting widow remarriage and education for women.
 
• It advocated monotheism, rational thinking, and a departure from idol worship and rituals.
 
 
 
• **Arya Samaj:**
 
 
• Founded by Dayanand Saraswati in 1875, Arya Samaj emphasized the Vedas as the ultimate source of knowledge and guidance.
 
• It advocated social reforms such as the abolition of caste discrimination, child marriage, and untouchability.
 
 
 
• **Bahujan Samaj:**
 
 
• This term is generally associated with the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP), founded by Kanshi Ram in 1984, to represent the Dalits, Adivasis, Other Backward Classes (OBCs), and minority communities.
 
• BR Ambedkar, a key Dalit leader and social reformer, laid the ideological foundation for movements advocating the rights of marginalized communities.
 
 
 
• **Jyotiba Phule's Contributions:**
 
 
• He was a social reformer, writer, and activist who challenged the caste system and gender inequality in India.
 
• He authored several important works, including "Gulamgiri" (Slavery), which critiqued the caste system and called for equality.

questions.question: Which law permitted widow remarriage in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hindu Widow Remarriage Act, 1856**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Hindu Widow Remarriage Act** was passed on **26 July 1856** during British rule in India.
 
• This act was enacted to **legalize the remarriage of Hindu widows**, which was previously considered a social taboo.
 
• It was championed by social reformer **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar**, who worked tirelessly to advocate for the rights of widows.
 
• The law provided widows with the legal right to remarry, addressing a major social injustice faced by women in traditional Hindu society.
 
• It played a key role in initiating **social reforms** and improving the status of women in 19th-century India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__

 
• **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar**

 
 
• A renowned social reformer and educationist, he was instrumental in advocating for widow remarriage.
 
• He persuaded the British authorities to pass the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act of 1856.
 
• Vidyasagar also worked to improve women's education and fought against child marriage.
 
 
 
• **Background of the Act**
 
 
• In traditional Hindu society, widows were often ostracized and denied basic rights, including remarriage.
 
• The act was introduced to address these injustices, providing widows with the legal right to rebuild their lives.
 
 
 
• **Key Provisions of the Act**
 
 
• The act legalized the remarriage of Hindu widows.
 
• It declared that children born from such remarriages would be considered legitimate.
 
• Widows forfeited their right to their deceased husband's property after remarriage.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Act**
 
 
• The act marked a significant step toward gender equality in India.
 
• It faced resistance from orthodox sections of society but paved the way for future social reforms.
 
• It is considered a landmark in the history of women's rights in India.
